newsitem.title: USA: NASA to rerun curtailed shuttle mission.
newsitem.headline: NASA to rerun curtailed shuttle mission.

text.p: The shuttle Columbia will return to space in July to complete a science mission cut short earlier this month by a faulty power generator, NASA officials said on Thursday.
Columbia, which ended its curtailed mission on April 8, would be readied for a rerun of the science mission in near-record time, NASA spokesman Bruce Buckingham said.
"It's going to be an aggressive schedule but it's something we think we can do," he said.
Columbia's blastoff from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre was tentatively scheduled for July 1, just 84 days after it landed.

Buckingham said the quick turnaround would be possible partly because the mission's experiment-packed science laboratory would remain aboard the shuttle. Columbia's seven member crew was to stay together for the second try.
Columbia's planned 16-day science mission was aborted after only four days aloft because of a problem with one of three electricity-generating fuel cells.
The mission featured 33 major 'zero gravity' experiments, including two to study the behaviour of fire in space. Only a fraction of the research was accomplished during the truncated flight.
Meanwhile, NASA engineers were meeting into the evening Thursday to decide how to deal with a problem that was holding up launch preparations for the shuttle Atlantis.
The space agency was looking at ways to strengthen protective caps over explosive devices that jettison the shuttle's strap-on fuel tank after launch.
Parts of the caps, made of titanium, have shown signs of distortion and possible metal fatigue.

Despite the last-minute troubleshooting, Atlantis remained on scheduled for a May 15 launch, NASA officials said. The shuttle is to pick up U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger from Russia's Mir space station and drop off his replacement.
